headline: Dry weather holds through most of Wednesday, then a fast-moving cold front brings bursts of heavy rain, gusty winds and possible thunderstorms late Wednesday night into Thursday, with about a quarter to half inch of rain in San Diego County and more to the north.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Tuesday night stays dry after Monday night's widespread soaking west of the mountains. Scattered clouds regather along the coast this evening, with a 20–30% chance of a low cloud deck at times, mainly between about 2 and 7 AM Wednesday, and high clouds spreading in Wednesday morning. In the mountains and deserts, west wind gusts of about 30–40 mph on the desert slopes and through the passes die down over the next few hours.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Wednesday stays dry for most of the day, with temperatures near normal along the coast and below normal farther inland. A storm diving down the West Coast pushes a cold front from northwest to southeast across the region starting Thursday morning; it is strongest in Orange and San Bernardino Counties and weakens as it reaches Riverside and San Diego Counties late Thursday morning or early afternoon, with a chance of thunderstorms. Rain can fall at 0.25–0.50 inch per hour in San Diego County (heaviest in North County) and 0.50–0.65 inch per hour farther north and in the mountains, enough for street flooding and ponding on roads, along with 30–35 mph gusts at the coast and valleys, so secure outdoor items and watch for falling tree limbs. Totals: 0.25–0.50 inch in San Diego County, 0.50–1 inch in Orange County and parts of the Inland Empire, 0.50–1.50 inches in the San Diego and Riverside mountains, 1–2 inches in the San Bernardino Mountains, 0.10–0.30 inch in the High Desert and 0.10 inch or less in the lower deserts; scattered showers linger through Thursday and a weaker disturbance could bring more light rain to northern areas Friday (timing uncertain). In the mountains and deserts, gusts of 50–60 mph hit the San Bernardino Mountains' ridges and desert slopes and 45–55 mph in the High Desert (Wind Advisory 11 PM Wednesday to 4 PM Thursday for the San Bernardino Mountains and Apple and Lucerne Valleys), and 40–55 mph in the Riverside and San Diego County mountains and passes, easing Thursday evening; snow levels stay above 7,000 feet during the heaviest rain, then drop to 6,000–6,500 feet Thursday afternoon and evening, with 3–5 inches above 7,500 feet and 1–2 inches below that.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Much of Friday and Saturday look dry, with temperatures staying near to below normal into early next week. Another round of unsettled weather is possible sometime Sunday or Monday, with most computer-model runs showing at least light rain west of the mountains. The timing and how far south that storm reaches are still uncertain, with more details expected in the coming days.

coast: A High Surf Advisory runs until 4 AM Wednesday for the Orange County and San Diego County coasts, driven by a mix of long- and short-period west-northwest swells. The shorter swell fades this evening, so surf drops briefly to 3–5 feet on Wednesday, then a new northwest swell raises surf again late Thursday into early Friday, with elevated to high surf at times through the week. Coastal flooding is expected at times this week because of the high surf, even with tides under 6.5 feet through Friday; King Tides peak next week, with tides over 7 feet possible starting Saturday, Nov. 21. For boaters, a Small Craft Advisory runs until 4 AM Wednesday with 20–25 knot gusts and choppy 4–7 ft seas (steep 7–10 ft seas south of San Clemente Island through Wednesday morning), easing afterward, before steep 7–10 ft seas and 20–30 knot gusts return Thursday into Friday morning, with winds turning from south-southwest to west by late Thursday afternoon.
watch_for: Bursts of heavy rain and 30–35 mph gusts as the front passes Thursday morning and early afternoon, with street flooding possible.
Possible thunderstorms within the front on Thursday.
Coastal flooding at high tide, with King Tides able to top 7 feet starting Saturday.
confidence: Forecasters are confident in dry weather through most of Wednesday and in Thursday's front, less sure about the timing of Friday's light showers, and uncertain about the timing and reach of the Sunday–Monday system.
